clean_title: @0x Sero's 14-hour timelapse update on AI model training and GPU benchmarking
summary:
timelapse #167 (14 hrs)
- was harder to focus today since so many X notifications were coming in
- for most of today i made fast progress by using grok (speed is no 1 for me) and having it ask codex and fable for advice where it wasnt sure. this advisor method WORKS. sometimes for hard problems ill ask it to give fable an optimization task in the background while it works on other things with me in the loop.
- got craftax full game in cuda to 12M sps at 3 mingru layers with hidden size 256 on rtx pro 6000
- did a few dozen looped transformer pre-trains today. at 1B params (dense, moe, loop, no loop), burning a ton of my pocket cash on 8xH100s
- filling up empty cells properly with fable 5 max, gpt 5.6 sol max, grok 4.5 high, kimi k3 max, opus 4.8 max ($1500 burned). publishing when all runs finish and when i audit all of em
- getting funding secured to maintain kernelbench and its expensive runs
- kicked off minecraft foundation model pre-trains for the night. unsure how they went (checking now)
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2078931176073662464/img/jV6rBfmW0FFxEdkf.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2078931176073662464/vid/avc1/480x270/_vP58W3nRp31wLgl.mp4?tag=29
clean_summary:
Timelapse of 14 hours. Focus was harder today due to many notifications. Fast progress was made using grok, which asks Codex and Fable for advice on uncertain problems, and this advisor method proved effective. Sometimes, hard problems prompt asking Fable to handle an optimization task in the background while working on other issues.

Full game of Craftax was trained in CUDA to 12 million samples per second with three Mingru layers, hidden size 256 on an RTX Pro 6000. Several dozen transformer pre-trains at 1 billion parameters (dense, MoE, loop, no loop) were run, using eight H100 GPUs and costing around $1500. The user is filling up empty cells with various models and plans to publish results after auditing.

Funding has been secured to maintain Kernelbench and its costly runs. Nightly pre-trains for a Minecraft foundation model were started, with results being checked now. A video shows the progress.

clean_summary: GLM-5.2 (744 billion parameters) is now running with a true 4-bit NVFP4 key-value cache on 4x DGX Spark hardware at 41 tokens per second. It achieves a peak decode rate of 42 tokens per second, with a 317K-token key-value pool that is 58.6% larger than fp8, and serves a 316K context window. The system is needle-verified at 250K depth and was built in a single night using custom Triton and CuTe kernels. This demonstrates significant performance improvements and efficient caching for large language models on high-end hardware.

title: @0x Sero
summary:
these are crazy numbers.
Quoting @elliotarledge
Laguna-S 2.1 NVFP4 on a single RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell 96GB.
Ubuntu 24.04, CUDA 13.2, vLLM 0.25.1, concurrency 1, 262k max context, CUDA graphs and FlashInfer. Target is NVFP4. The published DFlash-NVFP4 draft is actually BF16 according to its config. K=3 was the winner.
Benchmark: 32,732-token coding prompt, 1,024 output tokens, temp 0.7, top-p 0.95, 3 runs.
- 155.17 tok/s mean, 6.60 stdev
- 51.4% draft acceptance
- 156.10 tok/s on a subsequent live run
- 91.2GB VRAM used
- Full 262,144 context fits; throughput test was at 32k
Stock vLLM with the same setup did 145.12 tok/s. I have a small vLLM patch that keeps single-request FlashInfer sequence metadata on GPU instead of synchronously reading it back every step. That added 6.9% and cut GPU-empty time by 68%.
vllm serve poolside/Laguna-S-2.1-NVFP4 \
--trust-remote-code \
--tensor-parallel-size 1 \
--max-model-len 262144 \
--max-num-seqs 1 \
--gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 \
--speculative-config '{"model":"poolside/Laguna-S-2.1-DFlash-NVFP4","num_speculative_tokens":3,"method":"dflash"}' \
--enable-auto-tool-choice \
--tool-call-parser poolside_v1 \
--reasoning-parser poolside_v1 \
--served-model-name laguna \
--default-chat-template-kwargs '{"enable_thinking":true}' \
--override-generation-config '{"temperature":0.7,"top_p":0.95}' \
--host 0.0.0.0 \
--port 8000

title: @0x Sero
summary:
Most goated nerd
Quoting @MaxForAI
‼️突发：DeepSeek @deepseek_ai 创始人梁文锋在一场据称长达四小时的投资者会议上的发言内容曝光。
过去一个月里，这场对话的片段一直在中国 AI 圈和投资人圈内流传。
最引人注目的是梁文锋反复强调的“不”字。
不搞“天才”神话。
不追求利润最大化。
不搞闭源。
不盲目争夺用户。
不做视频生成、3D、世界模型，也不做下一个“超级应用”。
他的解释很简单：
“克制是一种策略。放弃一些东西，是为了提高实现 AGI（通用人工智能）的概率。”
以下是会议中的核心观点：
- DeepSeek只有一条主线：AGI
梁文锋认为，现在不是追求产品收益最大化的时候。
核心是追逐人工智能最高峰，即AGI。
他的AGI路线图非常清晰。
去年的台阶是思维链，今年的台阶是Agent。
Agent之后，是持续学习。
持续学习之后，是AI自我迭代。
然后，AI开始帮助人类研发更加先进的AI系统。
最后才是具身智能。
梁文锋将这个过程称为“渐进的奇点”。
根据这个思考，DeepSeek目前正在主动放弃许多热门方向。
“很多东西不在我们的主线上，包括3D和视频生成。”
他也质疑了世界模型的重要性：
“世界模型跟智能的上限没有太大关系。”
多模态对产品和C端用户很重要，但它仍然只是一个组件。
“它不是主线，也不是智能本身。”
- 下一代模型必须拥有持续学习能力
人类可以在工作中不断学习。
但AI每次开始一个新任务，都需要人类重新提供所有相关上下文。
“这几乎是不可能的。”
这也是梁文锋认为，当前AI还无法真正替代员工的原因。
“下一代模型必须具备持续学习能力，否则就不能叫下一代模型。”
同时他表示智能的终点可能是具身。
他的逻辑很简单：
人类真正需要的，并不是另一个计算机界面。
人类需要的是劳动力。
- DeepSeek不追求利润最大化
梁文锋表示，DeepSeek不会以收入最大化为目标进行定价。
“我们只赚一个合理的利润。”
DeepSeek V4最初担心需求过多，所以价格定得比较高。
后来，DeepSeek把价格降到了四分之一。
“公司群里很多人都在欢呼。”
因为做出这个模型的目的，就是让更多人能够充分使用它。
备受关注的低成本不仅是一种商业策略。
“低成本是架构带来的结果。”
更低的成本可以让AI变得更加普惠。
但还有一个更深层的原因：
单位计算成本越低，DeepSeek就越能够在有限算力下训练更大的模型。
“大公司可以通过增加资源解决问题，我们优先考虑成本效率。”
有意思的是梁文锋并不觉得API生意有多么好。
“我不觉得卖API这个事情有那么大的吸引力。”
DeepSeek只需要一个很小的团队维护服务。
几乎没有客服，也不需要销售，用户自己就会来。
“我们一直在商业化，只是不以商业化为目标。”
他认为，DeepSeek彻底转向商业化的时间点仍然非常遥远。
- 开源是DeepSeek的战略甜蜜点
对于员工来说，开源能够带来成就感和组织凝聚力。
对于社会来说，它能够帮助研究者、企业和普通用户。
“开源是一种让利。”
梁文锋认为，AI最终会成为一个规模极其庞大的产业，任何试图垄断它的人，最终都会失败。
“如果AI最终占到人类社会GDP的10%，任何想要独占这部分利益的人，都会被历史抛弃。”
梁文锋表示，DeepSeek不会开源一个较弱的版本，同时在内部保留更强的模型。
他不担心竞争对手部署DeepSeek模型。
小型创业公司可能缺乏资源和意愿，去进行前沿模型研究。
大型公司可能拥有资源，却存在组织上的困难。
梁文锋认为，DeepSeek刚好处于一个罕见的中间位置。
“这是属于我们这个规模公司的sweet point。”
- 中美AI的差距主要在资源
梁文锋认为，中国并不真正缺乏人才。
DeepSeek希望改写中美AI竞争的叙事：
用几分之一的算力，把差距缩短到6个月，甚至3个月。
他作出这个判断的原因是他依然相信Scaling
“我们相信Scaling，规模越大，效果肯定越好。”
DeepSeek训练当前规模的模型，并不是因为这个规模已经足够。
而是因为现有算力只允许它做到这个规模。
梁文锋认为，前沿模型的竞争，最终会由三个因素决定：
成本、时间、用户体验。
“成本排在第一位。”
如果两家公司提供的模型质量相同，胜负将取决于谁能以更低的成本提供服务。
时间排在第二位。
早几个月和晚几个月，结果可能完全不同。
用户体验可以形成一定的黏性和壁垒，但梁文锋并不认为它是最本质的护城河。
- 团队稳定是梁文锋唯一不能让步的事情
他将其视为DeepSeek面临的最大风险之一。
原话是：“只有一个是没法退让的：必须保持团队的稳定性。”
而最近的一轮融资，已经大幅降低了这个风险。
“只要能够保持团队的稳定性，我一定能做成AGI。就这么简单。”
有趣的是DeepSeek的组织既是自上而下，也是自下而上
自上而下的部分，被梁文锋称为“做正事”。
但他不希望被安排的工作占用员工一半以上的时间。
另外一半时间应该保持自下而上。
研究人员可以自由探索他们认为重要的方向，不需要提前审批，也没有固定要求。
与很多AI团队不同，DeepSeek不鼓励过度加班。
“做研究需要一个相对松弛的环境。”
另一个原因是聚焦。
DeepSeek的许多产品并不完善，但公司会主动选择不去补齐所有问题。
梁文锋认为，这同样是一种克制。
有趣的是DeepSeek靠愿景驱动，而不是KPI
“要实现某个KPI，不是我们的方式。”
梁文锋表示，DeepSeek的愿景甚至不一定被正式写下来。
它存在于公司的做事方式里，也存在于公司对待世界的态度里。
“愿景不是挂在墙上的标语，不是怎么说，而是怎么做。”
梁文锋最后的警告，可能也是最重要的一句话
“如果你的愿景是拿得更多，你就已经输了。你可能会面临更大的困难。这个世界就是这样。”
DeepSeek不想赢下每一个AI市场。
它想保留实现AGI所需要的专注、成本优势、团队稳定性和组织自由。
而梁文锋似乎愿意放弃几乎所有其他东西，只为增加实现AGI的概率。
他在做真正很Cool的事情。
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HN3E6esaEAABWF8.jpg

title: @0x Sero
summary:
I am seeing some surprise and dismay that several major U.S. companies have come out in support of open models and an implicit alliance between these firms and China.
I am surprised at the surprise, and it shows how much rhetoric has changed in the last few years, but U.S. firms doing business with Chinese companies has been the norm and aggressively promoted by U.S. policymakers since the 1990s.
It usually works like this: U.S. firms produce products and use Chinese firms either to assemble those products or to produce components of those products to U.S. specifications.
So, if you're an AI startup, you will be building an AI product that's going to have some of the following: an interface, a harness, some fine-tuning, some proprietary data, an LLM, and of course various hardware components.
If I am developing a product for XXX Corp and I'm focused on best results with lowest cost, a Chinese LLM might indeed fit the bill, because these are being offered at a lower cost. So of course a lot of SMEs are going to want the option of Chinese LLMs to produce a product they need even if it isn't the SOTA product off the shelf.
In some use cases, you don't want the state of the art! Imagine I have a temporary on-site office somewhere and I need furniture for the office. I'm not going to buy the best furniture on the market--that'd be a waste of money.
In business you buy what is cheapest and gets the job done--this is efficiency optimization. We denigrate this from the outside, so businesses in their marketing talk about no-expenses spared cutting-edge everything under the hood, but that is marketing. In reality, you do what is best for the particular job, including what is most economical and efficient.
So, it's not surprising that demand for low-cost open models will be overwhelming.
For a company like Meta, Nvidia, Microsoft, or Dell Technologies, they understand this. They know that they will have value in the AI ecosystem providing one bit of service or another, and a low-cost open-source LLM will expand demand for their products and services. It expands demand by allowing smaller businesses more access to AI solutions, and it expands demand by allowing all businesses more use cases where they can economically produce or implement an AI solution.
The only people who do not want this, and who will try to manipulate our legislators into not wanting this, are OpenAI and Anthropic.
Now, there is a solution.
If OpenAI and Anthropic give up on the "one big model" approach and an obsession with using Mercor et al. to pay flunkies to click "yes, this is good" on domain-specific outputs, they can design much more flexible products at lower cost that actually have product-market fit much more than what they're currently trying to do.
But they won't do that, because they're bewitched by a fantasy of ASI that is not real.
How do you go from claiming you need $7 trillion to reshape the global semiconductor industry to being a Software as a Service provider offering simple low-cost solutions to businesses? You can't, you just can't.
OAI and Anthropic painted themselves into a corner with their hyperbolic rhetoric.
Language matters.

clean_title: Kimi K3 runs on a Mac Studio M3 Ultra with open-source MLX port
summary:
Kimi on Mac Studio m3 ultra
Quoting @pipenetwork
Run Kimi K3 on a Mac Studio 🫰
K3 is 2.8T parameters and 1.6TB on disk, which makes it impossible to run on Apple Silicon.
Until now.
Our MLX port is now open source:
To accomplish this, we solved two things:
1. We wrote a streaming converter that walks one layer at a time, so that mlx_lm doesn't need to materialize the whole model.
2. REAP pruning sits on top and scores all 896 experts against a calibration corpus to keep only ones your workload needs.
That's what brings K3 down to 350GB and inside a Mac Studio.
clean_summary: Kimi K3, a 2.8 trillion parameter model that requires 1.6TB on disk, was previously impossible to run on Apple Silicon due to its size. Now, an open-source MLX port makes it feasible by using a streaming converter that processes one layer at a time, avoiding full model materialization, and REAP pruning that scores and keeps only the necessary experts for a workload. This reduces the model size to 350GB, enabling it to run inside a Mac Studio.

clean_title: Autoresearch and recursive optimization with LLMs for personal and industrial use
summary:
Most slept on repo of all time, anyone can autoresearch & deeply recursively optimise anything.
Do yourself a favor, get a cheap llm sub, or run something locally on some hardware, give it autoresearch and target it at something in your life.
- Budgeting
- Performance optimisations
- Resume & job application machine
- Local city/town mapping
- Clear all your personal info off the web
- Rebuild everything you pay for
I've been doing this for months, my life is infinitely better.
The concept is very very simple.
1. "Program.md": explain what it is you want, and what isn't allowed during autoresearch, especially great if u can define the output at each turn
2. "Prepare . py": a script that cleans up and enforces the experiment structure
3. Target: whatever it is you're trying to optimise, whether that's your email inbox, some mobile app/website you're trying to optimise load times for, or an llm training run.
4. Document and learn from the runs, this is practically free progress, if the run is designed as a ralph loop where the model is freshly instantiated at every turn even Qwen3.6-27B will work perfectly (heard from very trusted individuals.)
This can revolutionise so many industries and lives, I fully believe this with all my heart.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HOfN-iubYAA50kC.jpg
clean_summary:
Most overlooked repository of all time, anyone can use autoresearch and deep recursive optimization to improve various aspects of life or work.

The concept involves defining a goal and constraints in a 'Program.md' file, creating a 'Prepare.py' script to structure the experiment, and targeting any process or system for optimization, such as budgeting, performance, or web privacy. By documenting and learning from each run, even a model like Qwen3.6-27B can be used to make continuous progress, potentially transforming industries and personal routines.

clean_title: LLM compression techniques for local inference on high-end Macs
summary:
In pursuit of my goal to run Claude and GPT at home, here's what I've learned about LLM compression.
As my profile shows, I use LLMs a lot. Probably in the top 0.1% of all individual users. Imagine being a dealer's #1 customer.
If the dealer closes shop, you're fucked.
That's why I built this thing:
---------------------------
I've tried every model locally, every single one with over a thousand downloads on HuggingFace, in the pursuit of the one.
There are about 5 groupings at any point that are truly useful, but they're all lacking when you try them for serious work at this scale.
The most promising however for local inference are:
1. MiniMax-M2.1
2. GLM-4.7
These models got it right, excellent agentic behaviour and great coding. Great out the box with every harness, and are very easy to work with.
I had been able to use MiniMax-M2/.1 locally on my rig, but GLM-4.7 was just out of reach.
That's why I put this post up:
I spent this weekend pruning and quantizing models on Prime Intellect, their team was generous enough to give me 1000$ worth of credits.
---------------------------
My goal was simple, get both running on high end Macbooks, with full context at INT4 quants.
Why INT4?
Outside of exl3 quantizations as soon as you dip below 4bits you lose a lot of intelligence, unsloth quants are an exception to this rule..
However both EXL3 and GGUF quantizations are typically significantly slower than AWQ/GPTQ/Autoround
---------------------------
There's been a lot of good research into how we can take these behemoths and shrink them down to a reasonable size we can run on "consumer hardware" (anything that costs up to 10k usd)
Some of the top methods we have today include unsloth's work, and exl3
There's a big opportunity to further shrink this though, it was pioneered by Cerebras I believe.
---------------------------
Router-weighted expert activation pruning.
Mixture of Expert models are becoming the standard, very few labs have been launching dense models, which of course have their own pros and cons, one I'd like to call out for being excellent is Devstral-2
We can prune using a code and agentic heavy calibration set, which would help us identify which of the experts contribute the least to this kind of inference.
Then we can target how much we want to shave off the model, anything from 5% to 50%+ we can even reuse observations to do 5 prunes in a row.
What this means in practice:
1. We use a relevant dataset to see what is taking up unnecessary space
2. We chop off parts of the model that don't contribute to our goal
3. We have a much smaller model with nearly identical performance for our targeted workflows.
Cerebras put out a lot of high quality content around this idea, I will link them below.
Now that we've chopped off 50% of the model's experts, and the model is 50% smaller. We can move onto the next step.
---------------------------
Quantizing the model
Now that we have 50% of the model left, we know for a fact that only 5-10% of the model is being used during runtime.
Models are a set of configurations, and a list of 16 bit numbers, so another logic way to shrink the model is reduce the precision on some of those numbers.
A small amount of weights contribute the most to a model's outputs, and of course we are making a sacrifice here, but there's not much else to do.
We need to find the most important numbers, preserve them, then shrink the rest based on their importance.
So if we can get the right data to calibrate on we have a chance to further shrink the model down 75%, we make sure to reduce the precision of the weights that contribute least to our workflow.
---------------------------
Results
18 models are on my hugging-face, of which I have personally used 3 for 24-48 hours.
I was able to shrink GLM-4.7, and MiniMax-M2.1 down from:
720 GB ----> 92 GB (GLM)
460/230 GB ----> 62 GB (MiniMax-M2.1)
MiniMax-M2.1 200k context (4bit) = 96 gb
GLM-4.7 200k context (4bit) = 128gb
---------------------------
Of course we have 1-2 bit models but vibes tell me for the narrow use-cases you care about REAP + Quantization is the way to go.
I can now say I have Claude and GPT at home.
Sources & References:
- Cerebras REAP:
- Intel Autoround:
- Prime Intellect:

clean_summary:
In pursuit of running Claude and GPT models at home, @0xSero explores methods to compress large language models for local inference. They tested various models, focusing on MiniMax-M2.1 and GLM-4.7, which exhibit good agentic behavior and coding ability. Using pruning and quantization—particularly INT4 quantization—they managed to significantly reduce model sizes, shrinking GLM-4.7 from 720 GB to 92 GB and MiniMax-M2.1 from 460/230 GB to around 62 GB, enabling these models to run on high-end Macbooks with full context.

The process involves expert activation pruning to remove less contributing parts of the model, followed by weight quantization that preserves the most important weights while reducing precision for less critical ones. This approach leverages recent research into model shrinking techniques, making it feasible to run powerful models at home for a fraction of the original size. The goal is to make Claude and GPT models accessible for personal use, with an emphasis on cost-effective hardware and open-source tools.

I have a confession to make, I haven’t shared this openly online in a long time.
When I was in my late teens I just gave up on life, I felt like I would never do anything worthwhile.

I also stopped working, learning, or doing anything positive, on good days when i wasn’t going on benders I’d site at “home” playing the same 2 games over and over, smoking weed and drinking.
——————
When I was 4, I got my first computer and spent 3 hours a day unsupervised on the interwebs, going down “conspiracy theory pipelines” reading about gravity and physics, going onto lemon tube cause some forum posted it.
Needless to say I felt more intelligent than my peers, and maybe I was. So I gave up on school and would skip to go to cyber cafes all day.
This unfettered access to anything I can think of rotted my brain, but also made me aware that the world is much bigger than a class room.
——————
When I met my now wife, I was going through severe withdrawals. I didn’t want to keep doing what I was doing, but everyone I knew was a degenerate. It was hard to quit.
She let me move in with her, practically nursed me back to health over 2 years.
I had always had an interest in coding, specifically hacking and making computers do things they shouldn’t, but that was never nurtured.
——————
I decided now is the time, there will probably never be a chance to win again.

clean_title: Rubin Ultra’s HBM configuration reportedly down-speced due to supply constraints
summary:
A leading semi industry publication recently released a report (to institutional clients only) on how Rubin Ultra’s HBM config is reportedly down-speced from Rubin’s
That is, with performance maintained at 35 PFLOPs (NVFP4) –
HBM: from HBM4 (12-hi) to HBM4 (8-hi)
HBM capacity (per GPU): from 288GB (1 x 8 x 12 x 3) to 192GB (1 x 8 x 8 x 3)
HBM bandwidth: from 20TB/s to 21TB/s (noting that while Rubin is marketed as up to 22TB/s bandwidth, most will ship with 20TB/s at 9.7Gbps pin speed)
Other specs:
Scale-up size (# of GPUs): 72 to 576 (using NPO for inter-rack connections)
Chip TDP: from 1.8kW/2.3kW to 1.8/2.6kW
The 2.6kW SKU for Rubin Ultra is said to be offered as a max-performance variant. The 1.8kW variant, positioned to be mainstream, is designed with a max-Q profile optimized for energy efficiency & performance (per watt)
Back to memory –
The reason for the de-spec is purportedly due to constrained HBM supply, while also brings significant BOM cost reductions that offset the impact of upcoming HBM price increases
My take –
It’s interesting to hear about the HBM down-spec since HBM4E samples have already been shipped, as summarized below:
Samsung: announced the shipment of HBM4E samples on May 29 this year
(
Hynix: announced the shipment of HBM4E samples on 18 June this year
(
Micron: sometime next year (2027)
The specs for both Samsung’s and Hynix’s HBM4E samples are almost similar, i.e.:
Pin speed: 14 – 16Gb/s (Samsung); up to 16Gb/s (Hynix)
Interface/bus width: 2048-bit (standard)
Memory bandwidth/stack: ~3.6 – 4.0GB/s (Samsung); up to 4.0GB/s (Hynix)
Layer count/stack: 12
Capacity/layer: 4GB (up from 3GB in HBM4)
Total capacity/stack: 48GB (12 x 4)
It’s been widely reported that Rubin Ultra, expected to ship 2H 27, will come with HBM4E (rather than HBM4), so the timing of the sample shipments (from Samsung and Hynix) kinda checks out
In fact, if the HBM4E sample specs hold, assuming the 2-die/8 HBM stacks/GPU package config (same as Rubin, given reported CoWoS issues at TSMC for the 4-die/16 HBM stacks/GPU package config), then the memory capacity (per GPU package) should be at 384GB (1 x 8 x 12 x 4)
Of course, anything can happen over the next 12 – 18 months
As for scaling up to 576 GPUs, I think initial expectations were for NVIDIA to use Kyber rack architecture for this setup, but they did specify that multiple form factor development tracks exist (given challenges in engineering the ultra-dense midplane in Kyber)
A possible set up was mentioned in one of NVIDIA’s technical blogs where they’d demonstrated a Polyphe prototype (in the graphic below) using a two-layer all-to-all topology that can be used to combine 8 x MGX racks, each with 72 Rubin Ultra GPUs, into a single 576-GPU NVLink domain (using copper and direct optical connections. No mention about NPO)
They said that using this same MGX rack-scale ecosystem (already mature) allows them to achieve the fastest time to production

A recent report (for institutional clients) suggests Rubin Ultra’s HBM memory configuration is down-speced from earlier plans, with performance maintained at 35 PFLOPs. The changes include switching from HBM4 (12-high) to HBM4 (8-high), reducing per-GPU capacity from 288GB to 192GB, and slightly increasing bandwidth from 20TB/s to 21TB/s. Other specs, such as scale-up size from 72 to 576 GPUs and chip TDP from 1.8/2.3kW to 1.8/2.6kW, are also adjusted. The down-spec is attributed to constrained HBM supply and cost reductions that offset upcoming HBM price increases.

HBM4E samples, which are expected to ship in 2027 from Samsung and Hynix, have similar specs with 12 layers, 4GB per layer, and 48GB total capacity per stack. Rubin Ultra, expected in the second half of 2027, is likely to use HBM4E, which could provide 384GB per GPU package if the same stacking configuration is used. Scaling to 576 GPUs might involve a Polyphe topology with multiple MGX racks connected via NVLink, enabling dense inter-rack communication and faster deployment, as demonstrated in NVIDIA’s prototypes.

title: @0x Sero
summary:
I successfully local pilled Ben Davis.
Quoting @davis7
I've been using DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 through Pi a ton over the past few days and it's a pretty crazy feeling to have what's basically Opus 4.6 running in my closet.
I'll start with the downsides (b/c there are a lot of upsides):
1. This is a very expensive setup and is NOT something you should do to save money on subscriptions. I got this thing because I think it's really cool and I want to learn more about models, not to replace my frontier subs
2. It's still much weaker than the frontier in a lot of ways. The speed is worse since the model's less efficient, the actual intelligence is a lot lower, and you can't run more than 2-4 sessions at once. I'm often doing 20+ codex runs at once (counting sub agents) making this impossible for most real work
Issues aside tho, we've cross the threshold to where actually usable models for real work are not self host-able at home for less than $10,000.
One of the first things I tried was having it do the normal workflow I put a frontier model through:
1. Research the thing I'm asking for with subagents
2. Make a plan by asking tons of questions
3. Implement the thing
4. Review the thing with subagents
It did very very well.
As I was watching it it definitely overthought a lot of things and went in circles, but never fell apart. It always recovered itself and stayed on task. The actual code quality after doing the research was good, the functionality was what I wanted, and the design was solid.
The places where I think this thing actually makes a ton of sense are:
1. Anything involving the forbidden terms (bio, cyber security, etc.). I've been really surprised at just how much this model is willing to do. It never says no, I had it go crazy poking around my network and sites I've shipped, and never refused.
2. Any problem that just needs time to grind down (aka is verifiable). This is stuff like verifying something, quantizing a model, basically anything you can put in an auto research loop this thing will do really well.
Still need the frontier for more open ended tasks, but anything that can be brute forced is perfect for local models.
Been having a ton of fun with this thing and there's a ton more I want to try.

title: @0x Sero
summary:
A quick explanation for everyone excited about @0xSero’s DS4 edition:
I tested it on a DGX Spark, and the performance is real. Compared with DwarfStar, this stack delivers roughly 2.3× faster decoding and around 35% faster long-context prefill.
That sounds almost impossible, especially considering DwarfStar was built by the creator of Redis. But the key is that these are not actually the same model configuration.
DeepSeek V4 Flash is a mixture-of-experts model. Each layer contains 256 small expert networks, and for every token, a router selects the six most relevant experts, plus one shared expert that is always active.
In real-world workloads, expert usage is heavily skewed: some experts are activated constantly, while others contribute very little.
REAP retains 216 of the model’s 256 experts, pruning only the least-used 15.6%.
So the trade-off looks like this:
- DwarfStar: all 256 experts at roughly 2-bit
- @0xSero’s DS4: 216 experts—about 84%—at roughly 3-bit
Neither is the full-precision model, and each will likely lose capability in slightly different areas.
I’m still putting @0xSero’s build through its paces, but so far I’m loving the enormous performance boost on a single DGX Spark.

summary:
What a crazy day!
I quietly put live in the morning to make sure everything was working ahead of our announcement and get some early feedback on how people are using it in the wild.
Before I could get to the announcement, people discovered the website and the referral system and started sharing - on reddit, on group chats, on X. There was a race to get referrals to top the leaderboard. People who got referred, then referred more people, who referred even more people. Before I paused the website, there were 120 referral links being shared per hour on X alone. @MiaAI_lab was onboarding a user every ~10 seconds.
We discovered some bugs and got a lot of really great feedback through this unexpected mini-launch. We're going to take a day or two to integrate this feedback before we open up access again. We'll announce as soon as we do that on the @localdotai account. Then the race continues!
The website itself has over 350+ model configs tested on 10 different local devices, including DGX Spark, MacBook, Mac Mini, Mac Studio and RTX cards. It’s the most rigorous benchmark ever done for local hardware, with each model / hardware combination (3,500+) backed by 700+ real agent tasks (2M+ combinations). We then map out everything on cost, energy, end to end task time and intelligence. We spent close to $1M building this.
Thanks for bearing with us. Special thanks to @huggingface for powering the verification system. The Local AI community is amazing.

amazing work by Tom ❤️
Harness bundled with the inference engine
Quoting @tomgreenwald
Introducing Magnitude: your actually local agent
100% private and offline. No token costs, no API keys. Open source.
Today's agents are local. The model isn't. Every prompt, every file, every secret gets sent straight to Anthropic and OpenAI.
Magnitude is built around local models and runs the whole stack itself. The inference engine is part of the agent, so the models run inside it, right on your computer.
It lives in your terminal, and setup is one command. Magnitude profiles your hardware and shows you which models fit, with the trade-offs between quality, speed, and memory. Pick one and start working. No painful config or server to babysit.
Out of the box, it can use your shell, edit files, and run scripts. Add skills and it can work with Excel, PowerPoint, PDFs or Chrome.
Use it for everyday work:
- Analyze sensitive data
- Manage private notes
- Review code and logs
- Search and organize files
- Build docs or slides
npm i -g @magnitudedev/cli
GitHub:
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2085778414376767489/img/qwSMnGSEcEzIa3qV.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2085778414376767489/vid/avc1/360x270/MSsWFd2JKPN3I-UI.mp4?tag=29
clean_summary:
Amazing work by Tom. Magnitude is a local agent built around local models that runs the entire stack itself, including the inference engine, directly on your computer. It is 100% private and offline, with no token costs or API keys, and is easy to set up with one command.

The agent can use your shell, edit files, run scripts, and add skills to work with tools like Excel, PowerPoint, PDFs, or Chrome. It profiles your hardware to suggest models that balance quality, speed, and memory, making it suitable for analyzing sensitive data, managing private notes, reviewing code and logs, searching files, and building documents or slides. The setup is simple, and it can be used for everyday tasks without complicated configurations.

Local AI - some explorations
On Mac
Qwen3.6-27B · 4bit · 16 GB
Ornith-1.0-35B · 4bit · 20 GB
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B MoE · 4bit DWQ · 21 GB
Laguna-XS 2.1 · NVFP4 · 22 GB
Laguna-S 2.1 · OptiQ 2bit · 45 GB
Laguna-S 2.1 · oQ6e · 93 GB
DeepSeek-V4-Flash · 2bit DQ · 101 GB
On DGX Spark
DeepSeek-V4-Flash 0731 · IQ2XXS · 274 runs, plus an IQ3_XXS quant A/B
Qwen3.6-27B · NVFP4 · MTP speculation on and off
Laguna-XS 2.1 · NVFP4 · draft-model speculation on and off
Laguna-S 2.1 · NVFP4
and the spark got the knobs: 3 speculative drafters, thinking on and off, 4 reasoning effort rungs, prefill ladders out to 194k context, concurrency sweeps
here the general info about the tests im running,
a custom eval -
1,137 graded runs. 7 tasks. every run stamped with the same exam hash so the two machines can't drift apart
then i audited the exam itself
the 3 tasks that execute the model's code: trusted
the 2 that compare text by line position: broken
the 2 that check structure: one has a 46% floor, one is aced by everything
still determining the dimensions for model performance given hardware and tasks.
when working with constrained hardware understand current 'limitations' and how to push those is critical, yet just as critical to understand the time horizon of objectives. this means understanding how to go beyond tok/s optimization and optimize model behavior via a lightweight harness.
how do you begin to create integrated hw + objective optimizations per application? (for long running tasks)
open weight models are only 6mo behind from the frontier, yet if you can build a framework, a light weight harness, to re-enforce specific behaviors, you close that gap futher.

title: @0x Sero
summary:
This guy is incredible
Quoting @danpacary
new experiment: heterogeneous inference
macbook pro + DGX Spark.
the spark does prefill, the m4 max does decode. leveraging each box for what it is actually good at
starting with wifi tests, then moving to a wired 10gbe connection
why this split: the spark prefills DeepSeek at 1.5-2.3k tok/s and the mac's wall at long context is exactly prefill. and DeepSeek's cache is 86 KB per token = the one cache small enough to ship. qwen is 112, laguna is 160
the plan:
same GGUF byte-identical on both boxes
spark prefills -> writes the kv cache to disk (ds4 already does this, content-addressed files)
ship the file -> mac decodes a context it never read
shipping cost by context length, projected:
128k = 5.8 GB cache: ~60s wireless, ~5s over 10GbE
500k = 22.5 GB: ~4 min wireless, ~20s wired
1M = 46 GB: ~8 min wireless, ~42s wired
nothing wired is tested yet. these are projections
and the honest gap: most my prefill measurements stop at 32k. the interesting regime is 500k+. context-length testing is what comes next
the gate before any speed claim: a handed-off cache must produce 99% token-identical output vs prefilling locally. correctness first, then the speed

On my DS4-Flash recipe
It actually worked pretty fine, and was incredible fast, I could get 12 sessions in parallel comfortably.
But the dspark stuff that makes it so fast makes it likely that the model will incorrectly stream closing chat template structures.
Worse at longer contexts.
---------
Back to GLM-5.2
So i switched back to GLM-5.2 on the 6000s @ 180 tok/s for c1 and 500 tok/s c4
The sparks are doing mechanistic interpretability on Deepseek-v4-flash, with REAP observations, and J-Space
I'm feeding it every religious manuscript in every language I can get, and categorising activations and intermediate token states.
I am hoping my Switch comes in soon, they didn't approve the order, low stock. But when I do get it, 200 tok/s on DS4-Flash with DSpark on 4x sparks.
2 copies of DS4-Flash on each, 1 doing prefill only the other doing decode only.
-----------
I've been using ZCode tons for running goals with local models, unfortunately isn't stable for longer than 2 hour runs, I am working on slimming it down.
Litter is almost at a place where I'm happy with it, you'll see that it works now with localstudio in the latest version, but there's a lot of lag in long sessions, or in views with many sessions.
-----------
Local AI
It's been a pretty crazy 2 weeks, I've never had that many people use anything I worked on so heavily in such a short period of time.
Most of the software I built was dev scripts, enterprise agents, and consulting gigs on MVPs.
All that to say, things are setting back into a routine, and I am going to make sure it's the best website of it's type there is.
-----------
For my local rig, it's finally at a point where it's ripping 500M tokens a day, today I did 750M tokens, about 5% of it is a keeper, 15% of it is research and chats, the remaining 80% is churn through goals.
I am really optimistic that:
1. New hardware will enable billions to onboard
2. Models will get good enough and small enough
3. Hardware costs will ramp down over a few years
4. Most inference is going to be local
I don't really see a difference between frontier models and these behemoths I'm running, but the smaller ones like Nemotron Nano Lightning, Qwen, and Laguna, Gemma, and LFM are really maturing.
Anyway, thought I'd share

clean_summary:
I provided DS4-Flash with 22 million tokens of religious scriptures to see how models like GLM-5.2, GLM-5.3, Kimi-K3, and Opus-5 interpret them.

The results show that an expert model firing for all other religions does not activate for the Bible. Core scriptures like the Bible and Quran activate different expert circuits than later theological discussions and writings about these scriptures. Additionally, chants and rhymes use an average of 26 experts, while conversations and theology involve about 111 experts.

title: @0x Sero
clean_title: AI model intelligence and performance benchmarks on local hardware
summary:
Current methodology for those interested (see quoted post for detailed explanation).
Every point you see on this graph has 2649 end-to-end task runs behind it run with Hermes Agent, with a complete local environment.
How to read this chart: up is more intelligent, right is faster. The dotted line shows the Pareto Frontier.
This is just one device (DGX Spark).
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HPyftC3XAAI9BXm.jpg
Quoting @alexocheema
The intelligence score is currently a suite of evals (GDPVal, GAIA and tau2). It's a total of 883 unique tasks, run end to end in Hermes agent, for each model. We repeat each eval three times, giving a total of 2649 tasks per model. We take a weighted average across these eval scores to get the intelligence score. Coding is not represented well at all right now, but we're working on getting that added ASAP. One problem we have right now since we run so many tasks per model variation, is it takes a lot of compute and a lot of time to get them all done.
We want the numbers we present to be as representative as possible of what you as an end user will actually experience when you run AI locally on your hardware. We've made great care to ensure that by running the exact configurations you are able to run yourself locally, end-to-end, in the actual harness (Hermes Agent) with tool calls, web search, the full environment you would have locally.
Part of this is enabling users to view specific kinds of tasks. Once more evals are added, we will allow you to view by type of task (e.g. coding).
Bigger models are also being worked on. Internally we've run a lot of benchmarks on larger models with the DGX Station (GB300), with models like GLM-5.2, MiniMax M3, Inkling, Nemotron 3 Ultra, etc... Adding larger models very soon, which will be particularly interesting to users who have 512GB M3 Ultra or Multi-GPU.
Thanks @MiaAI_lab for all the support and your feedback is much appreciate!
clean_summary: This post discusses the current methodology for evaluating AI model intelligence using Hermes Agent across end-to-end tasks. Each point on the graph represents 2,649 tasks run locally on a DGX Spark device, with the evaluation suite including GDPVal, GAIA, and tau2, covering 883 tasks repeated three times for a total of 2,649 tasks per model. The scores are a weighted average of eval results, aiming to reflect real user experiences when running AI locally, including tool calls and web search. The post also mentions ongoing work to incorporate larger models like GLM-5.2, MiniMax M3, Inkling, and Nemotron 3 Ultra, especially for users with high-memory or multi-GPU setups. The linked benchmarks compare AI model performance, speed, energy use, and hardware across Apple silicon and NVIDIA GPUs.

linked_urls.title: Test Sieve and Give Us Feedback
linked_urls.summary: Sieve just won our local AI browser extension bounty 🏆 Announcement here: https://x.com/i/status/2089377946066932187 Now let's see how it holds up in the real world. ## The challenge Install Sieve, use it during your normal browsing, and put it through its paces. GitHub here: https://github.com/Phineas1500/sieve-ai-image-detector Try it across different websites, image types, and browsing scenarios. Look for things that work especially well, things that don't, false positives, false negatives, confusing UX, performance issues, or anything else that could make Sieve better. Then: 1. **Post your experience publicly on X.** 2. Share what you tested and what you learned. Make sure to tag @sriramkiron, @0xSero, and @kennyistyping when you post. 3. Include specific, actionable feedback wherever possible. 4. After you post, submit a claim on this page with a screenshot of your post + its URL in the claim description. Your feedback doesn't need to be positive. **We're looking for honest feedback that helps make Sieve better.** ## What makes a great submission? The most valuable feedback will be specific and actionable. For example: * Finding a type of AI-generated image Sieve consistently misses * Finding a type of real image it incorrectly flags * Identifying a performance or loading issue * Discovering a confusing part of the user experience * Testing Sieve on an interesting real-world browsing scenario * Suggesting a concrete improvement that makes the extension more useful The more you can demonstrate what you found and why it matters, the better. ## The prize This is a **winner-take-all bounty**. The winner will be the submission that bounty contributors **find most useful and that leads to meaningful improvements to Sieve**. This isn't a popularity contest or a writing competition. The goal is to find the feedback that actually makes the product better. ## Why we're doing this The first bounty helped create Sieve. This one is about putting it in the hands of real people and creating a feedback loop between users and the person building it. If Sieve is going to become a reliable, convenient, freely available public good, it needs to be tested against the messy reality of how people actually browse the web. So go break it. 🔍 Try Sieve, share what you find, and help make the next version better.

clean_title: @0x Sero on Sieve: a revolutionary tool for detecting AI-generated art
summary:
Just tried out Sieve today and I can say it is very revolutionary at aiding the deslopping of the web, for those who don't want to read ahead below is the link to the project:
First thoughts, for many this will be hard to install, I would recommend anyone going to use this to set their agent up to the repo, get the build path on their computer, then load the extension in their browser with "chrome://extensions", I feel as though eventually going through the chrome webstore process would greatly aid traffic and use of this project amongst the non vibers. But for less experienced vibers using github actions to build the zips for this developer extension would aid many also.
My Experience:
I took it too many "art sites" where AI imagery is common in cases where people share their AI art instead of real art it was very performant, however in cases where it had false negatives and through inspection I knew the "art" was AI generated I wished there was a way users could report anonymously and support further training of the model.
Next, I noticed that in the case of loading a page it decided to scan all the photos on an individual page where in some cases I prefered to be able to select one image to scan individually, rather than the visual clutter of all the loading bars.
Final wishes, due to the high accuracy of this model I feel as though a mode to just remove all slop art from the web would be a neat addition, as instead of an adblocker it would be a slopblocker.
I would like to thank @0xSero for sponsoring this project, and want to congratulate @sriramkiron for winning the big prize! Final thanks too @kennyistyping for being a legend and making poidh amazing!
clean_summary: @0x Sero shares their experience with Sieve, a tool designed to aid in identifying AI-generated images on the web. Installation may be challenging for some users, but setting up the extension via the repo or GitHub Actions can help more people use it. The tool performs well on AI art sites, though false negatives can occur, and user reporting could improve the model. Sieve scans all images on a page by default, but selecting individual images for scanning might be preferable. A future mode to block all AI-generated or 'slop' art could turn Sieve into a 'slopblocker,' serving as a specialized ad blocker. The project is sponsored by @0xSero, with congratulations to @sriramkiron for winning a prize, and thanks to @kennyistyping for their contributions.

clean_summary: DeepSeek v4 Flash 0731 operates at speeds comparable to GPT-5.6-Sol, offering 400k context for use in one or more sessions. It was tuned to protect coding experts and can serve as a creativity machine on a single Spark. The model is optimized for a single stream session with EXL3 quantization, 384k (conservative) to 440k (kv cache) context, 47 tokens per second structured, and 1024 tokens per second prefill. It passed a 370k token stability test, thanks to native NVFP4 KV cache and kernel bug fixes in upstream prefill. This setup enables reliable code generation with high speed and context, making it suitable for intensive coding tasks.

clean_summary:
How did @MiaAI_lab and @0xSero achieve similar speeds to 27b 8-bit models? They ported DeepSeek v4 Flash 0731 to MLX for test runs, enabling high-quality code generation, high context, and fast performance on a single DGX Spark.

The setup uses EXL3 quantization, supports 384k to 440k token context, achieves 47 tokens per second in a structured single stream, and passed a 370k token stability test. This is made possible by native NVFP4 KV cache and kernel bug fixes in the upstream prefill path, delivering quality comparable to Q4_K_M or Q5 GGUF models.

Leave your laptop in a café and come back to find a stranger guarding it.
Expect this everywhere from now on. Get your laptop stolen in Berlin 3 months later because Poland has completely destroyed your survival instincts.
Get a full dental cleaning for 30 dollars. Go twice a year now because there's no financial punishment for taking care of yourself. Become the healthiest version of yourself against your will.
Speak one word of Polish at a restaurant and watch the entire staff treat you like a son who just came home from war. Everybody is so friendly when you try their language that it feels unprofessional. You'll get used to it. Then you'll miss it everywhere else.

A weekend project costing around $50 and taking 4 to 8 hours to complete. The goal is to train a GPT2-level model, covering topics like datasets, Chinchilla, provisioning compute, training, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and benchmarks. Karpathy's YouTube series is recommended as a helpful resource.

Training Andrej Karpathy’s Nanochat on 4 RTX 3090s at 225W each is about 12.6% complete after 6.78 hours, with a loss of 3.14 and a throughput of 3,600 tokens per second. The process is stable with no errors, and the total cost is approximately $15 for 55 hours of training. The setup maintains temperatures between 52-57°C and uses 19GB of VRAM per card.

The repository used is NanoGPT, a simple and fast tool for training and fine-tuning medium-sized GPT models.
